I'll avoid further account-wide list calls to prevent surfacing more of that unrelated client's data. Let me get the exact webhook field name from Vapi's public docs instead (no account data involved) and continue the build.

Yes — this changes the architecture decision. The important issue is not the Domino’s/Wendy’s naming mismatch by itself; it is that **development automation and a real production voice assistant appear to share the same Vapi organization/API credential and therefore the same administrative blast radius**.

Also, the current Vapi documentation confirms the webhook configuration you were looking for. Vapi now uses the assistant’s **`server` object**, specifically **`assistant.server.url`**, rather than the older top-level `serverUrl` pattern. Vapi documents the hierarchy as tool server → assistant server → phone-number server → organization server. citeturn856956search3turn856956search6

For example, conceptually your yoga assistant should have its own configuration containing `server.url`, its own credential reference, and its own selected `serverMessages`. Vapi recommends using a **Custom Credential referenced through `credentialId`** instead of putting authentication secrets directly into webhook configuration. citeturn856956search4

More importantly, I would change your **MCP Control Plane / desktop automation architecture** now:

| Layer | What to do |
|---|---|
| Vapi Production | Existing restaurant/client assistants |
| Vapi Dev/Sandbox | Yoga, experiments, demos, development |
| API credentials | Separate DEV / STAGE / PROD credentials |
| MCP Gateway | Never expose unrestricted Vapi API directly to agents |
| Resource registry | Maintain explicitly approved assistant IDs |
| Read operations | `GET /assistant/{approved-id}` only |
| List operations | Block `/assistant` enumeration in production |
| Create | Allowed only in DEV namespace/account |
| Update | Require assistant-ID allowlist |
| Delete | Human approval + production lock |
| Tool creation | Environment-specific |
| Knowledge bases | Client-specific isolation |
| Phone numbers | Separate by environment/client |
| Webhooks | Separate endpoint per client/environment |
| Secrets | Vault/secret manager, not source code |
| Audit | Log caller, operation, assistant ID, before/after |
| Deployment | DEV → test → approval → PROD |
| Rollback | Store previous assistant configuration/version |

The control plane should effectively enforce:

```text
VS Code / Codex / AI Agent
          |
          v
   MCP Control Plane
          |
          +--> Identity
          +--> Policy Engine
          +--> Environment Resolver
          +--> Resource Allowlist
          +--> Approval Engine
          +--> Secret Manager
          +--> Audit / Trace
          |
          v
      Vapi Gateway
       /       \
      /         \
 DEV Vapi      PROD Vapi
 Yoga/Demo     Real Clients
```

A request such as:

```text
"Update my yoga inbound assistant"
```

should **not** translate into:

```text
GET /assistant
find something that looks right
PATCH it
```

It should translate into something deterministic:

```text
Project = SOHAM_YOGA
Environment = DEV
ResourceType = VAPI_ASSISTANT

Registry lookup:
SOHAM_YOGA.DEV.INBOUND
    -> assistant_id = <explicit registered ID>

Policy:
PATCH assistant/{registered-id} = ALLOW
GET /assistant = DENY
DELETE assistant/* = DENY

Execute
Audit
Verify
```

That eliminates the exact failure mode you just encountered.

One other detail matters for your integration build. Vapi's server events arrive as HTTP `POST` messages under a `message` object. Events can include transcripts, call status, tool calls, end-of-call reports and other conversation data. Some events require your server to respond, including `assistant-request`, `tool-calls`, and transfer-related requests. citeturn856956search0turn856956search2

So for the **Yoga Vapi webhook**, I would use:

```text
assistant.server.url
       |
       v
https://voice-dev.yourdomain.com/vapi/webhook
       |
       v
Webhook Gateway
       |
       +-- authenticate request
       +-- validate assistant ID
       +-- validate environment
       +-- validate event schema
       +-- redact PII
       +-- generate trace ID
       |
       +--> transcript processor
       +--> appointment/calendar
       +--> CRM
       +--> SMS / WhatsApp
       +--> payment-link workflow
       +--> analytics
       +--> audit store
```

Then configure only the `serverMessages` the yoga workflow actually needs rather than indiscriminately subscribing to everything. Vapi exposes `serverMessages` precisely for selecting the events sent to your server. citeturn856956search5

### One additional issue I would flag

The **"Domino's Pizza-Inbound Call" assistant carrying Wendy's content** deserves a separate configuration-integrity check. It could simply be an old test/name reuse, but in a real production environment it can also indicate **configuration drift**: assistant identity, system prompt, knowledge base, tools, telephone number, branding and deployment metadata may no longer correspond.

I would therefore add a permanent **Configuration Drift Guard** to your AI Control Tower:

```text
Expected configuration
        |
        v
Git / Configuration Registry
        |
        +----------------------+
        |                      |
        v                      v
Expected Assistant        Vapi Runtime Assistant
        |                      |
        +----------COMPARE-----+
                   |
        +----------+-----------+
        |          |           |
      Prompt      Tools       KB
      Model       Voice       Number
      Brand       Webhook     Credentials
        |
        v
PASS / WARNING / CRITICAL
```

That is actually a strong real-world use case for the **AI Control Tower + MCP Control Plane** architecture you've been designing: **preventing one AI developer/agent/project from accidentally discovering, modifying, deleting, or deploying into another client's production environment.**

And yes: avoiding further account-wide `GET /assistant` calls is appropriate **for now**, but I would not regard that as the final security control. The durable solution is **account/environment isolation + least-privilege credentials + explicit resource IDs + policy enforcement + audit trails**.

# 2. The most important Vapi → VS Code webhook

### `assistant-request`

This is extremely useful for your architecture.

Instead of hardwiring one assistant to every phone number:

```text
Incoming Call
     ↓
Vapi
     ↓
assistant-request
     ↓
Your MCP / Webhook Gateway
     ↓
Routing Engine
     ↓
Who is calling?
What phone number?
Which company?
Which language?
What time?
Existing customer?
Reason for call?
     ↓
Choose Assistant
```

For example:

```text
403-xxx-1111
      ↓
Soham Yoga

403-xxx-2222
      ↓
Dental Clinic

403-xxx-3333
      ↓
Restaurant

403-xxx-4444
      ↓
Physiotherapy
```

Your backend can return the appropriate `assistantId` dynamically.

Vapi requires an `assistant-request` response within **7.5 seconds end-to-end**, so this router needs to be lightweight and deterministic. citeturn509457search1

---

# 3. Tool-call webhook

This will probably become the **largest integration point** in your system.

Customer:

> “Book me for yoga tomorrow at 6 AM.”

Vapi:

```text
Conversation
   ↓
LLM determines action
   ↓
tool-calls
   ↓
Your MCP Gateway
```

Then:

```text
Tool Router

bookAppointment()
      ↓
Google Calendar

createCustomer()
      ↓
CRM

sendConfirmation()
      ↓
SMS / WhatsApp

takePayment()
      ↓
Stripe

updateAnalytics()
      ↓
Control Tower
```

Vapi supports custom tool/function calls where the Server URL receives the requested function and parameters and returns a result to the assistant. citeturn509457search1turn509457search5


# 8. Transfer scenarios

You should implement several human handoff reasons:

```text
customer_requests_agent
AI_low_confidence
customer_angry
payment_problem
emergency
medical_question
legal_question
policy_exception
VIP_customer
repeated_failure
tool_failure
authentication_failure
unsupported_request
```

Vapi supports a `transfer-destination-request` where your server can determine the transfer target dynamically. citeturn509457search1

This lets you create:

```text
Caller
 ↓
AI
 ↓
Transfer Router
 ├── Sales
 ├── Billing
 ├── Reception
 ├── Instructor
 ├── Manager
 └── Emergency fallback
```

# 9. Transcript webhooks

Extremely useful for your **AI Control Tower**.

You can receive transcript events during the conversation. citeturn509457search1

```text
Vapi Transcript
      ↓
Event Bus
      ↓
Real-time AI Evaluation
      ├── Sentiment
      ├── Intent
      ├── Toxicity
      ├── PII
      ├── Hallucination
      ├── Compliance
      ├── Agent quality
      ├── Customer satisfaction
      └── Escalation risk
```

You do **not necessarily want Claude reacting to every partial token**. That becomes costly and adds latency.

Better:

```text
partial transcript
→ lightweight rules

final utterance
→ evaluation

end-of-call
→ deep Claude evaluation
```

---

# 10. End-of-call webhook

This should be one of your most important events.

Vapi provides `end-of-call-report`, including call information and potentially artifacts such as transcript/messages and recording information. citeturn509457search1

Your pipeline:

```text
Call ends
   ↓
end-of-call-report
   ↓
Event Processor
   ├── store transcript
   ├── update CRM
   ├── summarize conversation
   ├── extract action items
   ├── evaluate AI
   ├── evaluate customer
   ├── calculate KPIs
   ├── identify failures
   ├── identify hallucinations
   ├── estimate cost
   └── trigger follow-up
```

This is where your **VS Code + Claude architecture becomes powerful**.

```text
Vapi
 ↓
End Call Report
 ↓
Observability Store
 ↓
Claude Evaluator
```

```text
Prompt problem
Tool problem
API problem
```

```text
Evidence
```

```text
Automated tests

        ↓

        ↓
```

# 12. Hang webhook

Vapi has a `hang` event designed to signal when the assistant has failed to respond for some time. citeturn509457search0turn509457search1

Very valuable:

```text
hang
 ↓
Control Tower
 ↓
Measure:
 - LLM latency
 - tool latency
 - STT delay
 - TTS delay
 - network delay
 ↓
Alert
```

Then Claude can investigate the trace.

```text
Vapi

Knowledge Request
```

For advanced projects, Vapi also supports dedicated custom voice server handling with `voice-request`. citeturn509457search1

```text

Hindi voice
Punjabi voice
```

# 16. Dynamic endpointing

Vapi also exposes specialized endpointing requests for custom detection of when the customer has finished talking. citeturn509457search1

This is very relevant to problems you previously identified:

```text
Customer:
"My credit card is
four five six seven...
[short pause]
eight nine..."

DO NOT treat pause
as finished speech.
```

Your endpointing service can make that smarter.

Vapi currently also supports **phone-number hooks** for `call.ringing`; supported actions include things such as `say` and `transfer`. citeturn509457search6

```text

 ↓

business hours?
maintenance mode?

emergency routing?
```

# 21. Webhook security scenarios

Every webhook needs:

```text
Authentication
Credential validation
Schema validation
Timestamp validation
Request logging
Rate limiting
Idempotency
Replay protection
PII masking
Environment validation
Assistant allowlist
Phone-number allowlist
Tool allowlist
Timeout
Circuit breaker
Retry policy
Dead-letter queue
Audit trail
```

Vapi currently supports Custom Credentials and recommends referencing them via `credentialId`; its authentication options include mechanisms such as bearer token, OAuth 2.0 and HMAC. citeturn509457search9

## Why B2B and B2C should be separated

B2C usually cares about individual customers, appointments, purchases, reviews, payments, retention, and service satisfaction.

B2B cares more about companies/accounts, decision-makers, contracts, quotations, opportunities, pipelines, renewals, account health, multiple contacts, and larger deal value.

So the core entities are different:

| Area | B2C | B2B |
|---|---|---|
| Primary entity | Individual | Company / Account |
| Contact model | One person | Multiple contacts |
| Sales cycle | Short | Longer |
| Purchase | Transaction | Opportunity / Contract |
| Pricing | Standard/package | Negotiated/tiered |
| Decision maker | Customer | Buyer + influencer + approver |
| Follow-up | Reminder | Multi-stage pursuit |
| Revenue | Purchase value | Account/deal value |
| Retention | Repeat purchase | Renewal/account expansion |
| Payment | Card/link | Invoice/PO/terms |
| Support | Individual case | Account-wide support |
| Reporting | Customer behavior | Account/pipeline performance |

Yes. In a Vapi-style architecture, you can handle **both inbound and outbound calls through webhooks**, but the webhook events are mostly **call lifecycle/runtime events**, not necessarily separate “inbound webhook” and “outbound webhook” products.

For inbound:

```text
Customer calls your number
        ↓
Vapi receives call
        ↓
Webhook / Server URL events
        ↓
Your Gateway
        ↓
CRM / Calendar / Payment / Notifications
```

Typical inbound events include call ringing/status changes, dynamic assistant routing, transcript updates, tool calls, transfers, interruptions, call end, and end-of-call reports.

For outbound:

```text
Your system / campaign / CRM
        ↓
API creates outbound call
        ↓
Vapi places call
        ↓
Same webhook gateway receives runtime events
        ↓
Status / transcript / tool / result / end report
```

So outbound usually starts with an **API-triggered call**, while inbound starts with a **customer dialing your number**. After the call exists, many webhook events are shared.

A clean design is:

```text
POST /webhooks/vapi/events
```

and then route internally by:

```text
call.direction = inbound / outbound
call.id
assistant.id
phoneNumber.id
customer/tenant
campaign.id
```

You can also separate them operationally:

```text
/webhooks/vapi/inbound
/webhooks/vapi/outbound
```

but I would normally recommend **one secured webhook gateway + internal direction router** rather than duplicating the entire integration stack.

The main distinction is:

| Capability | Inbound | Outbound |
|---|---|---|
| Call initiated by | Customer | Your platform |
| API needed to start call | Usually no | Yes |
| Dynamic assistant routing | Very important | Usually campaign-selected |
| Ringing/status events | Yes | Yes |
| Transcript events | Yes | Yes |
| Tool calls | Yes | Yes |
| Calendar/CRM/payment | Yes | Yes |
| Human transfer | Yes | Yes |
| End-of-call report | Yes | Yes |
| Campaign ID | Usually no | Very important |
| Retry/no-answer logic | Limited | Very important |
| Voicemail handling | Possible | Very important |

## 25. Missing NFRs I would explicitly add

A few that are often forgotten:

- **Idempotency** — duplicate webhook/tool calls must not double-book or double-charge.
- **Consistency** — CRM/calendar/payment state must not diverge.
- **Data durability** — no loss of critical audit or transaction records.
- **Graceful degradation** — if RAG fails, don't hallucinate; if calendar fails, send booking link or create callback.
- **Backpressure** — queues should protect systems during traffic spikes.
- **Rate-limit resilience** — provider quotas should not cause cascading failure.
- **Fairness/resource isolation** — one tenant cannot exhaust capacity for others.
- **Configuration correctness** — right customer, assistant, prompt, phone number and tools.
- **Determinism for transactions** — booking/payment/refund operations use workflows, not free-form LLM behavior.
- **Evidence completeness** — disputes/incidents must retain sufficient evidence.
- **Version compatibility** — APIs, MCP schemas, prompts and tool contracts.
- **Dependency concentration risk** — know when one vendor is a single point of failure.

To save tokens on Vapi, treat token optimization as an **architecture problem**, not just “make the prompt shorter.” The biggest savings usually come from reducing what you send to the LLM on every turn, routing simple work away from large models, and keeping deterministic business logic outside the prompt.

## Token-saving strategy

| Area | Waste pattern | Better approach |
|---|---|---|
| System prompt | Large prompt repeated every turn | Keep a compact core prompt |
| Knowledge | Entire FAQ/manual stuffed into prompt | Use RAG and retrieve only top relevant chunks |
| Conversation history | Full transcript resent | Summarize older turns |
| Tools | Huge tool schemas | Expose only tools needed for current intent |
| Model choice | Large model for every request | Route simple calls to smaller/cheaper model |
| Workflow | LLM decides every step | Use deterministic workflow engine |
| Customer context | Full CRM/customer profile injected | Fetch only required fields |
| Script | Entire script tree in prompt | Load scenario block dynamically |
| Policies | All policies always injected | Use policy service/guardrail lookup |
| Output | Long natural-language answers | Short voice responses |
| Repeated facts | Business details repeated every turn | Store in call/session state |
| Tool results | Full API JSON returned to LLM | Return minimal normalized result |

## 1. Keep the Vapi system prompt small

Bad:

```text
20-page company information
+
all services
+
all products
+
all prices
+
all policies
+
all FAQs
+
all escalation rules
+
all appointment logic
+
all payment logic
+
all CRM mappings
```

That gets expensive because much of it can be repeatedly supplied to the model.

Better:

```text
ROLE
You are the AI receptionist for {{business}}.

GOALS
Understand intent.
Answer only from approved information.
Complete allowed workflows.
Escalate when uncertain.

RULES
Do not invent facts.
Do not expose internal information.
Never collect raw card information.
Use tools for transactions.
Confirm successful tool execution before promising completion.

STYLE
Short conversational answers.
Usually 1–2 sentences.
Ask one question at a time.
```

Then retrieve the rest only when needed.

---

# 2. Dynamic prompt loading

Do not give every caller every scenario.

Use:

```text
CALL
 ↓
Intent Detection
 ↓
Scenario Router
 ↓
Load only required prompt block
```

Example:

```text
Caller:
"I need to change my appointment."

Load:
Appointment Rescheduling Module

Do NOT load:
Sales
Payment
Complaint
Survey
Renewal
Product catalog
Outbound campaign
```

This can reduce prompt size dramatically.

---

# 3. Use hierarchical prompts

I recommend:

```text
CORE PROMPT
~ small permanent instruction set

        +

TENANT PROMPT
business-specific identity/rules

        +

SCENARIO PROMPT
booking/payment/sales/etc.

        +

DYNAMIC CONTEXT
only current customer/task data
```

Conceptually:

```text
CORE
500 tokens

TENANT
300 tokens

SCENARIO
400 tokens

CURRENT CONTEXT
300 tokens

TOTAL
~1,500 tokens
```

Instead of continuously carrying a 7,000–15,000 token prompt.

---

# 4. RAG instead of knowledge stuffing

This is probably one of your biggest savings.

Bad:

```text
System Prompt
+
100 FAQs
+
pricing catalog
+
service descriptions
+
refund policy
+
location details
+
manual
```

Better:

```text
Question
   ↓
Intent
   ↓
Search approved knowledge
   ↓
Retrieve 2–4 relevant chunks
   ↓
Rerank
   ↓
Send only best evidence to LLM
```

For:

> “What is your cancellation policy?”

Send just:

```text
Cancellation policy:
Appointments cancelled with less than 24-hour notice...
```

Not the whole business knowledge base.

---

# 5. Tight retrieval budget

Do not blindly configure RAG like:

```text
Top-K = 20
```

You may end up injecting thousands of useless tokens.

Start with something like:

```text
Retrieve 8
 ↓
Rerank
 ↓
Return top 2–4
```

And enforce:

```text
Maximum RAG context tokens
Maximum chunk count
Minimum relevance score
```

For many voice interactions, 2–3 strong chunks are better than 10 mediocre chunks.

---

# 6. Keep chunks small but meaningful

Not too tiny, not giant.

For business Voice AI, logical chunks often work better:

```text
FAQ answer
Service description
Pricing rule
Cancellation policy
Location
Opening hours
Promotion
Procedure step
```

Rather than arbitrary huge pages.

Example:

```text
Service: Massage Therapy
Duration: 60 minutes
Price: $95
Buffer: 10 minutes
Cancellation: 24 hours
```

This compact structured representation is much cheaper than retrieving a 1,500-word brochure.

---

# 7. Put structured facts in DB, not RAG

Very important.

Do not use an LLM+RAG query for:

```text
Price
Business hours
Appointment availability
Customer balance
Order status
Inventory
Payment status
```

Use structured APIs.

```text
Question:
"What time do you close?"

Business Hours API
→ 8 PM
```

Instead of:

```text
Embedding
→ Vector search
→ 6 chunks
→ LLM interpretation
```

Faster, cheaper, more accurate.

---

# 8. Minimize conversation history

Voice conversations generate a lot of history.

Instead of sending:

```text
Turn 1
Turn 2
Turn 3
...
Turn 38
```

Use:

```text
Recent 4–8 turns
+
Conversation Summary
+
Structured State
```

Example summary:

```text
Customer wants physiotherapy.
Prefers Friday afternoon.
Price concern.
Offered 2:00, 3:30, 4:30.
Customer currently considering 4:30.
```

That may replace thousands of historical tokens.

---

# 9. Maintain structured session state

This is even better than prose summaries.

```json
{
  "intent": "appointment_booking",
  "service": "physiotherapy",
  "preferred_day": "Friday",
  "preferred_period": "afternoon",
  "price_objection": true,
  "selected_slot": null,
  "sentiment": "neutral"
}
```

Then inject only the fields needed by the next step.

---

# 10. Use an external state machine

Your architecture should look like:

```text
LLM
 ↓
Intent

Workflow Engine
 ↓
State

LLM
 ↓
Conversation
```

Do not make the LLM remember everything through chat history.

Example:

```text
state = WAITING_FOR_SLOT_SELECTION
```

Then the prompt only needs:

```text
Customer was offered:
2 PM
3:30 PM
4:30 PM

Ask which they prefer.
```

---

# 11. Reduce tool schemas

This is a hidden token problem.

If you expose 30 tools:

```text
CRM tools
Calendar tools
Payment tools
Messaging tools
Order tools
Support tools
Marketing tools
```

their definitions can consume significant prompt context.

Instead:

```text
Intent = Appointment
```

Expose only:

```text
check_availability
book_appointment
reschedule_appointment
cancel_appointment
```

When:

```text
Intent = Payment
```

Expose:

```text
get_payment_status
create_payment_link
```

This is **dynamic tool exposure**.

---

# 12. Create one gateway tool where appropriate

Instead of many verbose tool schemas:

```text
crm_get_customer
crm_create_customer
crm_update_customer
crm_add_note
crm_change_status
crm_create_task
crm_get_history
```

you can sometimes expose a compact MCP/gateway interface such as:

```text
customer_action
```

with controlled operations behind the gateway.

But don't overdo this. A giant generic tool schema can become ambiguous. Use a small number of well-designed domain tools.

---

# 13. Normalize tool responses

Bad tool response to LLM:

```text
Entire Salesforce object:
120 fields
metadata
timestamps
IDs
audit fields
nested relationships...
```

Good:

```text
{
 "found": true,
 "name": "John",
 "customer_status": "active",
 "open_appointment": false
}
```

The gateway should strip irrelevant fields before sending results back to the model.

---

# 14. Don't send raw calendar responses

Same problem.

Provider returns:

```text
500 lines JSON
```

Gateway converts it to:

```text
Available:
14:00
15:30
16:30
```

That saves tokens and reduces hallucination risk.

---

# 15. Smaller model for intent routing

You don't need your premium model for:

```text
Book appointment
Cancel appointment
Opening hours
Payment status
Human transfer
```

Architecture:

```text
Incoming utterance
      ↓
Small Router Model
      ↓
Simple?
 ┌────┴────┐
YES       COMPLEX
 ↓          ↓
Small      Large
Model      Model
```

Potential model classes:

```text
Tier 1
classification/router

Tier 2
standard voice conversation

Tier 3
complex complaint/reasoning

Tier 4
human
```

---

# 16. Deterministic answers where possible

For:

> “What time are you open today?”

you might not need generative reasoning at all.

```text
Hours API → "We’re open until 8 PM today."
```

For:

> “Your appointment is Friday at 3:30 PM.”

Template the response.

This reduces both token usage and unpredictability.

# 17. Use response templates

Examples:

```text

"You're booked for {{date}} at {{time}}."

PAYMENT:
"I've sent the secure payment link by {{channel}}."

TRANSFER:
"I'll connect you with {{department}}."
```

No need for a 200-token model response every time.

Voice responses should usually be short anyway.

Prompt instruction:

```text

Ask only one question at a time.
Do not repeat information unless the caller asks.
```

Bad:

> “Certainly, I would be more than happy to assist you today with your appointment scheduling request…”

Good:

> “Sure. What day works best for you?”

Both better UX and fewer output tokens.

Voice agents often waste tokens on:

```text
Certainly!
I'd be happy to help.
Thank you for providing that information.
```

on every turn.

Set:

```text

Use them only when socially useful.
```

Cache:

```text

Locations
Service catalog
Price catalog
Staff names
Common FAQs
Holiday hours
```

Architecture:

```text
Request
 ↓
Cache?
 ├─ HIT → answer
 └─ MISS → source system → cache
```

This primarily saves API/RAG workload but can also reduce repeated retrieval context.

---

Example:

Previous:

> “How much is massage therapy?”

New question:

> “What's the cost for a massage?”

Architecture:

```text
 ↓
Semantic Cache
```

Use it only for safe/stable content, not dynamic data.

```text
                        ↓

                        ↓
```


For your platform, the major principle should be:

> **Vapi generates the conversational intent; the Communication Layer decides whether, what, when, where, and to whom a message is actually delivered.**

That keeps messaging controlled, auditable, cheaper, tenant-safe, and much easier to scale.
